chunks: From him, from Safwan, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said:
I asked Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who buys food from another man when it is not yet in his possession, so he buys it from him immediately. He said: 'There is no harm in it.'

I said: 'Indeed, they invalidate it among us.' He said: 'And what do they say about al-salam (forward sale)?' I said: 'They see no harm in it. They say: This is for a specified term. So if it is for no term and is not in the possession of its owner, then it is not valid.'
He said: 'If there is no specified term, it is better.'
Then he said: 'There is no harm in buying food when it is not yet in the possession of its owner, for a specified term.'

He said: 'He should not specify a term for it, unless it is a sale of something like grapes and watermelon and similar items that are not found in their season, so it is not appropriate to buy those immediately.'

key_terms.أَجَل: Specified term or deadline for delivery or payment.
key_terms.أَجْوَدَ: Better or more excellent (in legal context).
key_terms.السَّلَم: Forward sale (Salam), a contract where payment is made in advance for goods to be delivered later.

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on selling food that is not yet in the seller's possession?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) validates the permissibility of selling food not yet in possession, aligning with the broader Shia jurisprudence on *bay' al-salam* (forward sale). He distinguishes between general goods, where an unspecified term is preferable, and perishables like grapes and watermelon, which require immediate sale to avoid uncertainty (*gharar*). This ruling reflects the practical economic needs of the community while maintaining strict adherence to the conditions of validity in commercial transactions.
